Text: TCP uses {{c1::Socket}} and {{c2::ServerSocket}} for connection-oriented communication, while UDP uses {{c3::DatagramSocket}} and {{c4::DatagramPacket}} for connectionless packet delivery.
Extra: TCP guarantees ordered delivery via a handshake; UDP sends packets independently with no session.

Text: The TCP three-way handshake consists of three messages: {{c1::SYN}}, {{c2::SYN-ACK}}, and {{c3::ACK}}, allowing client and server to synchronize {{c4::sequence numbers}} before data transfer.
Extra: Without synchronized sequence numbers, TCP cannot detect missing or duplicate packets.

Text: `ServerSocket.accept()` {{c1::blocks the calling thread}} until a client connects, so it should always run on a {{c2::worker thread or thread pool}}, not the main thread.
Extra: Running accept() on the main thread freezes the whole application while waiting.

Text: Failing to close a socket causes a {{c1::file descriptor (FD) leak}} at the OS level, eventually throwing {{c2::SocketException: Too many open files}} and {{c3::BindException: Address already in use}} on restart.
Extra: The OS kernel holds FD entries open until the socket is explicitly closed or the process exits.

Text: `new URL(String)` was deprecated in Java {{c1::20}} because it triggers a {{c2::DNS lookup}} inside the constructor, which violates basic API design rules by performing {{c3::blocking network calls}} during object construction.
`URI` performs {{c1::strict RFC 2396 syntax-based parsing}} without resolving hostnames, whereas `URL` may perform {{c2::DNS lookups}} in methods like `equals()` and `hashCode()`.
Extra: This makes URI safe to use in collections, while URL in a HashMap silently causes network calls.

Text: `HttpURLConnection` default timeouts are {{c1::infinite (0)}}, meaning an unresponsive server will {{c2::block the calling thread forever}} unless `setConnectTimeout()` and `setReadTimeout()` are explicitly set.
Java 11 `HttpClient` was introduced by JEP {{c1::321}} and supports {{c2::HTTP/1.1}} and {{c3::HTTP/2}} with automatic fallback, plus {{c4::WebSockets}}.
Extra: HttpClient is designed as an immutable, thread-safe singleton shared across the application.

Text: `HttpClient.sendAsync()` returns a {{c1::CompletableFuture<HttpResponse<T>>}} immediately without blocking. The response is delivered via {{c2::callback}} when the I/O completes on the internal event loop.
`HttpURLConnection` is hardcoded to {{c1::HTTP/1.1}} and lacks {{c2::HTTP/2 multiplexing}}, {{c3::async request support}}, and modern {{c4::header compression}}.
Extra: These limitations are exactly the motivations for the Java 11 HttpClient.

Text: The Java pattern `try (Socket s = ...; InputStream in = ...) {}` guarantees that resources are closed in {{c1::reverse declaration order}} even if {{c2::multiple exceptions}} are thrown during cleanup.
Extra: This prevents FD leaks that would occur if manual finally blocks were skipped due to exception handling.

Text: In the client-server model, the {{c1::client}} initiates the connection while the {{c2::server}} binds to a port and {{c3::listens}} for incoming requests.
Extra: Java mapping: `new Socket(host, port)` → client; `ServerSocket.accept()` → server side.
